sections.h2: What is a 1031 exchange for a Florida property owner?
sections.html:
A 1031 exchange lets an investor who sells real property and buys replacement real property report the swap on Form 8824 instead of reporting a taxable sale. The IRS instructions for that form say the rules now reach exchanges of real property only, and the property must be held for business or investment rather than lived in as a main home. A Florida rental house, a small apartment building or vacant land held as an investment can all be the "given up" property, and the replacement does not have to sit in Florida.

The exchange is a federal tax matter. Florida adds its own paperwork, mainly the deed and the county clerk's recording of it, which are covered further down this page. Anyone who lives in the house they are selling should read the home sale exclusion page for the main residence rules, since that tax break works differently.

You must name the replacement property in writing within 45 days after you transfer the property you give up, and you must receive it by the earlier of 180 days after that transfer or the due date, with extensions, of your tax return for that year. Both clocks start on the closing date of the sale, and the IRS instructions give no extra time for weekends or holidays.

The written identification has to describe the replacement in a clear and recognizable way. For real estate, the instructions accept a legal description, a street address or a distinguishable name such as the name of an apartment building. The signed document must reach the person who is to transfer the replacement property to you, or another person involved in the exchange who is not a disqualified person, before the 45th day ends. Alternatively, every party can sign one written agreement naming the property by that date.

  • Day 0: closing on the Florida property you are giving up.
  • Day 45: last day to identify replacement property in writing.
  • Day 180, or the return due date with extensions if sooner: last day to receive the replacement.

Because the 180-day period can be cut short by the return due date, an owner who closes late in a year should ask a tax professional whether to extend the return so the full period stays available.

sections.h2: Do you need a qualified intermediary in Florida?
sections.html:
In a deferred exchange, where the sale and the purchase close on different days, using a qualified intermediary is the common structure, and the IRS says an exchange run through one is still treated as a like-kind exchange. The seller never takes hold of the sale money. The intermediary holds it and uses it to buy the replacement property.

The Form 8824 instructions warn that if you miss the timing rules because of the intermediary, the deal can fail as a deferred exchange and the gain may be taxable in the year you transferred the property. They also describe a qualified exchange accommodation arrangement for cases where the replacement is acquired first. Ask the intermediary how it protects your funds and what happens if a deadline is missed, and read the exchange agreement before you sign it.

sections.h2: Which Florida properties qualify and which do not?
sections.html:
Real property held for investment or business use qualifies, and personal property such as furniture or equipment no longer does. Your own home does not qualify as the property given up. The IRS instructions include a section on property used as a home and on property used partly as a home, so a duplex where you live in one unit needs a careful split.

  • Likely to qualify: a rented single-family house, a small multifamily building, commercial space, farmland or raw land held for investment.
  • Unlikely to qualify: your main residence, a home held for quick resale as inventory, or a condo you use as a vacation home.
  • Needs advice: a property you rented out but also stayed in, since the use mix drives the answer.

The instructions also say incidental personal property that goes with the real estate is acceptable only within a 15 percent limit of the replacement property's fair market value. Furnished rentals are worth raising with the tax adviser before you list.

sections.h2: What happens if you swap with a relative or related company?
sections.html:
Special rules apply, and an exchange built to avoid them is treated as a sale. The IRS defines a related party to include your spouse, child, grandchild, parent, grandparent, brother or sister, and certain related corporations, partnerships, trusts, estates and tax-exempt organizations. The rule also reaches a swap made through an intermediary, and a swap made by a single-member LLC that you or a related party owned.

If you do a related-party exchange, you must file Form 8824 for the year of the exchange and for the two years after it. Florida investors who keep property in family LLCs should list every owner before they pick a replacement, because a swap with a related party on the other side can change the tax result.

sections.h2: What Florida closing items still apply to a 1031 sale?
sections.html:
The Florida deed is taxed like any other sale deed. The Department of Revenue says the documentary stamp tax on a deed is 70 cents per $100 of consideration in every county except Miami-Dade, where the printed rate is 60 cents plus a surtax that does not apply to a document that transfers only a single-family dwelling. All parties to the document are liable for the tax, even though the contract decides who pays it.

The deed is recorded with the clerk of the circuit court, and the recording fee schedule in section 28.24 of the Florida Statutes sets the page charges. A deed also has to be signed in front of two witnesses under section 689.01. For the tax side of the closing, the Department of Revenue's documentary stamp page lists which deeds are taxable.

sections.h2: How do Florida closing costs, federal timing and the exchange fit together?
sections.html:
Key rules for a Florida 1031 exchange
ItemRule as printed by the source
Identify replacementIn writing within 45 days after transfer (IRS Form 8824 instructions)
Receive replacementEarlier of 180 days or return due date with extensions (IRS)
Property typeReal property only after the regulations (IRS)
Related partyFile Form 8824 for the exchange year and two years after (IRS)
Deed stamp tax70 cents per $100 outside Miami-Dade (Florida Department of Revenue)

Ask your Florida title agent or closing attorney how the intermediary will receive funds, since the exchange paperwork has to be in place before the sale closes.

faqs.q: Can I do a 1031 exchange on my Florida home?
faqs.a: Not on a main residence. The IRS rules apply to real property held for business or investment, and the Form 8824 instructions give separate treatment to property used as a home. If you lived in the house, look at the home sale exclusion instead and ask a tax professional about any rental period.

faqs.q: Is there any extension of the 45-day or 180-day deadline?
faqs.a: The 180-day period ends early if your tax return is due sooner, and an extension of the return can keep the full period open. The IRS instructions describe no extra days for weekends or holidays, so count calendar days from the closing.

faqs.q: Does Florida require a separate form for a 1031 exchange?
faqs.a: Ask the clerk or your title agent if any county form applies. You report the exchange on federal Form 8824 with your return, and the deed and its stamp tax follow the usual Florida closing steps through the clerk of the circuit court.

faqs.q: Do I pay documentary stamp tax when I sell the old property?
faqs.a: Yes, the deed is taxable. The Department of Revenue lists warranty, special warranty and quitclaim deeds among taxable documents, and all parties are liable for the tax even if the contract assigns it to one side. Ask your closing agent which party pays under your contract.

faqs.q: Can I buy replacement property in another state?
faqs.a: The IRS instructions do not tie replacement property to Florida. The IRS instructions speak of like-kind real property and ask filers to note the country when real property is outside the United States. Confirm the details of an out-of-state purchase with your intermediary.
